question: Find the part with an error: Each of the branch managers have (A) / been asked to submit (B) / a quarterly compliance report. (C)
explanation: 'Each of' takes a singular verb, so 'have' should be 'has'.

question: Find the part with an error: The chairman, as well as (A) / the directors, were present (B) / at the annual general meeting. (C)
explanation: With 'as well as', the verb agrees with the first subject: 'was'.

question: Find the part with an error: The loan was sanctioned (A) / after the borrower had furnished (B) / all the necessary informations. (C)
explanation: 'Information' is uncountable and has no plural.

question: Find the part with an error: The board has approved (A) / the merger, subject to (B) / the regulator's consent. (C)
explanation: The sentence is correct; 'subject to' is followed by a noun phrase.

question: Find the part with an error: The furnitures (A) / for the new branch (B) / arrived last week. (C)
explanation: 'Furniture' is uncountable and has no plural form.

question: Find the part with an error: The new policy aims at (A) / providing credit to farmers which (B) / have no collateral to offer. (C)
explanation: 'Who', not 'which', is used for persons.

question: Find the part with an error: The bank's net profit (A) / this year is higher (B) / than last year. (C)
explanation: Like must be compared with like: 'than last year's' or 'than that of last year'.

question: Find the part with an error: Scarcely had the auditors (A) / begun their inspection when (B) / the records went missing. (C)
explanation: 'Scarcely had ... when' is the correct pattern.

question: Find the part with an error: Being a rainy day, (A) / the customers stayed away and (B) / the branch remained almost empty. (C)
explanation: The participle dangles; it should be 'It being a rainy day'.

question: Find the part with an error: She was so tired that (A) / she could not hardly (B) / keep her eyes open. (C)
explanation: 'Hardly' is negative; 'not hardly' is a double negative.

question: Find the part with an error: He has not (A) / yet decided whether he (B) / will accept the offer or no. (C)
explanation: 'Whether ... or not' is the correct form.

question: Find the part with an error: Only after the results were declared (A) / did the candidates realise (B) / how tough the competition had been. (C)
explanation: 'Only after' at the start correctly triggers inversion.

question: Find the part with an error: Lest he should not (A) / miss the train, (B) / he left home an hour early. (C)
explanation: 'Lest' is already negative, so 'not' must be dropped.

question: Find the part with an error: The bank will (A) / provide loans to whomever (B) / meets the eligibility criteria. (C)
explanation: The pronoun is the subject of 'meets', so 'whoever' is needed.

question: Find the part with an error: The suggestion was (A) / welcomed by everyone (B) / except he. (C)
explanation: 'Except' is a preposition and takes the objective case 'him'.

question: Find the part with an error: Little did the borrower know (A) / that the bank had already (B) / initiated recovery proceedings. (C)
explanation: Negative adverb 'little' at the start correctly takes inversion.

question: Find the part with an error: Supposing if the loan (A) / is not repaid on time, (B) / the guarantor will be held liable. (C)
explanation: 'Supposing' and 'if' are redundant together; use one of them.

question: Find the part with an error: He is one of the most (A) / intelligent officer that (B) / the bank has ever recruited. (C)
explanation: 'One of the most' takes a plural noun: 'officers'.

question: Find the part with an error: Neither the manager (A) / nor his assistants (B) / was present at the review. (C)
explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'assistants'.

question: Find the part with an error: Neither the cashier nor (A) / the tellers were informed (B) / about the system upgrade. (C)
explanation: The verb correctly agrees with the nearer subject 'tellers'.

question: Find the part with an error: He denied to have (A) / taken any bribe from (B) / the contractor. (C)
explanation: 'Deny' is followed by a gerund: 'denied having'.

question: Find the part with an error: The audit team returned (A) / back to the head office (B) / after completing the inspection. (C)
explanation: 'Returned back' is redundant; 'back' must be dropped.

question: Find the part with an error: Hardly a day passes (A) / without some new scheme (B) / being announced by government. (C)
explanation: 'The government' needs the definite article.

question: Find the part with an error: So severe was the drought (A) / that the government had to (B) / waive farm loans in several districts. (C)
explanation: 'So + adjective' at the start correctly takes inversion.

question: Find the part with an error: The scissors is lying (A) / on the table beside (B) / the cash counter. (C)
explanation: 'Scissors' is a plural noun and takes 'are'.

question: Find the part with an error: The quality of the (A) / mangoes this season are (B) / far superior to last year's. (C)
explanation: The subject is 'quality', which takes 'is'.

question: Find the part with an error: The policy will benefit (A) / not only the farmers (B) / but also to the traders. (C)
explanation: 'Not only ... but also' needs parallel structure; drop 'to'.

question: Find the part with an error: Should you need (A) / any further assistance, please (B) / contact the branch manager. (C)
explanation: 'Should you need' is a correct inverted conditional.

question: Find the part with an error: Every boy and every girl were (A) / given a scholarship (B) / under the new scheme. (C)
explanation: Subjects joined by 'and' but preceded by 'every' take a singular verb.

question: Find the part with an error: The customer insisted (A) / on to meet the manager (B) / before signing the papers. (C)
explanation: 'Insist on' is followed by a gerund: 'on meeting'.

question: Find the part with an error: She did not like (A) / the movie, and (B) / neither I did. (C)
explanation: After 'neither', the subject and auxiliary invert: 'neither did I'.

question: Find the part with an error: The committee, which comprises (A) / five senior officers, has (B) / submitted its final report. (C)
explanation: 'Comprises' needs no 'of', and the collective noun takes 'has' and 'its'.

question: Find the part with an error: The poor needs (A) / immediate relief more than (B) / long-term promises. (C)
explanation: 'The poor' refers to people in general and takes a plural verb.

question: Find the part with an error: Many a student (A) / have failed to clear (B) / the preliminary examination. (C)
explanation: 'Many a' takes a singular noun and a singular verb: 'has'.

question: Find the part with an error: The new recruits were (A) / asked to avoid (B) / to use their phones during training. (C)
explanation: 'Avoid' is followed by a gerund: 'using'.

question: Find the part with an error: It was not until the loan (A) / was disbursed that the farmer (B) / could buy the seeds. (C)
explanation: 'It was not until ... that' is a correct cleft construction.

question: Find the part with an error: One of my friend (A) / has joined the State Bank (B) / as a probationary officer. (C)
explanation: 'One of' is followed by a plural noun: 'friends'.

question: Find the part with an error: The new manager (A) / is very much popular (B) / among the junior staff. (C)
explanation: 'Very' modifies a positive adjective; 'very much' is wrong here.

question: Find the part with an error: The economy is expected (A) / to grow faster this year (B) / than it did in last year. (C)
explanation: No preposition is used before 'last year'.

question: Find the part with an error: Under no circumstances (A) / will the bank disclose (B) / a customer's account details. (C)
explanation: 'Under no circumstances' correctly triggers inversion.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Bank failures can wipe out the savings of ordinary depositors overnight.
Q. This assurance helps prevent panic withdrawals whenever a bank runs into trouble.
R. Under it, each depositor's balance is protected up to a fixed limit, currently five lakh rupees.
S. To guard against this, India set up a deposit insurance scheme through the DICGC.
explanation: P states the risk, S the remedy, R explains it ('under it'), Q gives the benefit.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. It also allowed businesses to claim credit for taxes already paid on inputs.
Q. The Goods and Services Tax was introduced to replace this patchwork with a single levy.
R. As a result, the cascading effect of 'tax on tax' was largely eliminated.
S. Before 2017, goods moving across state borders attracted a maze of separate taxes.
explanation: S gives the old problem, Q the reform, P adds a feature, R the result.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. On his fourth attempt, he finally cleared the exam with a comfortable margin.
Q. Determined not to fail again, he began reading an editorial every morning.
R. Within a year, his vocabulary and reading speed had improved markedly.
S. Each time, he fell short in the English section by a handful of marks.
T. Ravi had attempted the bank's probationary officer exam three times without success.
explanation: The story runs in time order: T, S, Q, R, P.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Rising sea temperatures, however, cause corals to expel the algae that feed them.
Q. Yet they support nearly a quarter of all known marine species.
R. Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor.
S. Without these algae, the corals turn white and eventually die, a process known as bleaching.
explanation: R and Q ('yet') describe reefs, P the threat, S follows with 'these algae'.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Earlier, a cheque deposited in one city had to be physically carried to the drawee bank.
Q. Clearing can now be completed within a single working day.
R. This often delayed clearing by several days.
S. The Cheque Truncation System replaced this paper journey with an electronic image.
explanation: P the old process, R its drawback, S the replacement, Q the improvement ('now').

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Antibiotics transformed medicine in the twentieth century.
Q. Some infections that were once easily treatable are now life-threatening again.
R. Their overuse, however, has allowed bacteria to evolve resistance.
S. Health experts therefore urge doctors to prescribe these drugs only when essential.
explanation: P introduces, R the problem ('their'), Q its effect, S the advice ('therefore').

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. In 1930, the British government held a monopoly on the manufacture and sale of salt.
Q. The act inspired millions across the country to join the civil disobedience movement.
R. He marched with his followers from Sabarmati to the coastal village of Dandi.
S. There, he picked up a handful of natural salt, breaking the law openly.
T. Gandhi chose to defy this law as a symbol of resistance.
explanation: P sets the context, T 'this law', R the march, S 'there', Q the impact.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Compound interest, on the other hand, is charged on the principal plus accumulated interest.
Q. Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal.
R. Over long periods, this difference becomes enormous.
S. That is why financial planners advise people to start saving early.
explanation: Q and P contrast the two, R 'this difference', S the conclusion.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. They pollinate a large share of the crops that humans eat.
Q. Bees are vital to global food production.
R. Scientists blame pesticides, habitat loss and disease for this decline.
S. In recent decades, however, bee populations have declined sharply.
T. Unless the trend is reversed, food prices could rise significantly.
explanation: Q states the importance, P explains it, S the decline, R 'this decline', T the warning.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Within months, it had opened tens of millions of zero-balance accounts.
Q. The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana was launched in 2014 to address this gap.
R. Millions of Indian households once had no access to a bank account.
S. These accounts later became the channel for direct benefit transfers.
explanation: R the gap, Q the scheme, P its reach ('it'), S 'these accounts'.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. This is because concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night.
Q. Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside.
R. Planting trees and creating green roofs can help reduce it.
S. This trapped heat creates what is known as the urban heat island effect.
explanation: Q the observation, P the cause, S 'this trapped heat', R the remedy.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Recovery proceedings were then initiated under the SARFAESI Act.
Q. When he failed to respond, the account was classified as a non-performing asset.
R. The bank, accordingly, sent him a formal notice demanding repayment.
S. The borrower had missed three consecutive EMIs on his home loan.
explanation: The events follow in sequence: S, R, Q, P ('then').

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Its author is traditionally believed to be Kautilya, an adviser to Chandragupta Maurya.
Q. Kautilya drew on his experience at the Mauryan court to cover subjects as diverse as taxation, espionage and diplomacy.
R. The Arthashastra is an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft.
S. His insights into statecraft are still studied by students of political economy today.
explanation: R names the text, P its author, Q its content, S its legacy ('his').

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Phishing calls have become a common tool of cyber fraudsters.
Q. Such a caller typically poses as a bank official and asks for an OTP.
R. Banks therefore remind customers never to disclose an OTP to anyone.
S. Once the victim shares it, the money is siphoned off within minutes.
explanation: P introduces, Q 'such a caller', S 'it' (the OTP), R the advice.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Its members pool small savings every month into a common fund.
Q. Over time, banks also begin lending to the group as a whole.
R. A self-help group usually consists of ten to twenty women from the same village.
S. From this fund, loans are given to members who need money urgently.
explanation: R defines, P 'its members', S 'this fund', Q the later stage.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Many of them discovered that productivity did not fall as feared.
Q. The pandemic forced companies across the world to let employees work from home.
R. Some have consequently made remote work a permanent option.
S. Critics, however, warn that it may weaken team culture over time.
explanation: Q the trigger, P the discovery, R the consequence, S the caveat.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. In a coal-dependent grid, therefore, the overall emissions may not fall much.
Q. Their environmental benefit, however, depends on how the electricity is generated.
R. Electric vehicles produce no tailpipe emissions.
S. Hence, the shift to electric vehicles must go hand in hand with cleaner power generation.
explanation: R the claim, Q the qualification, P the example ('therefore'), S the conclusion.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. The grateful owner, an elderly teacher, offered him a reward, but Anil politely declined.
Q. Inside it were several thousand rupees and an identity card.
R. While walking to the bank one morning, Anil found a wallet lying on the pavement.
S. Using the address on the card, he reached the owner's house that evening.
T. He decided to trace the owner instead of keeping the money.
explanation: The story runs in time order: R, Q, T, S, P.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Sometimes even a sound bank may face a sudden shortage of cash.
Q. In such situations, the central bank steps in as the lender of last resort.
R. This prevents a temporary crisis from turning into a full-blown collapse.
S. It provides emergency liquidity against eligible collateral.
explanation: P the problem, Q 'in such situations', S how it helps, R the outcome.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. As a result of this unchecked pumping, the water table in many districts is falling by nearly a metre each year.
Q. Free electricity has encouraged them to pump water without restraint.
R. Punjab's farmers rely heavily on tube wells for irrigation.
S. Experts warn that parts of the state could face desertification within decades.
explanation: R the practice, Q the cause, P 'this unchecked pumping', S the warning.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. The game later travelled to Persia, where it acquired the name shatranj.
Q. Chess is believed to have originated in India around the sixth century.
R. From there it spread to Europe, evolving into the modern game.
S. Known then as chaturanga, it represented the four divisions of an army.
explanation: The history runs in order: Q, S ('then'), P ('later'), R ('from there').

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. In 2019, the government announced the merger of ten public sector banks into four.
Q. Stronger balance sheets, it was argued, would enable them to lend more and compete globally.
R. Unions, however, opposed the move, fearing job losses.
S. The aim was to create fewer but larger banks with stronger balance sheets.
explanation: P the announcement, S the aim, Q the argument, R the opposition.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Users then share them without pausing to check the source.
Q. Media literacy programmes aim to break this cycle.
R. This is partly because sensational claims provoke stronger emotions.
S. Fake news spreads faster on social media than verified reports.
explanation: S the fact, R the reason, P 'them' (the claims), Q 'this cycle'.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Lakshmi ran a small tailoring shop from her home.
Q. A local bank sanctioned her a loan under the MUDRA scheme.
R. Within a year, her monthly income had nearly tripled.
S. She wanted to buy two more sewing machines but lacked the funds.
T. With the new machines, she hired two assistants from her neighbourhood.
explanation: The story runs in order: P, S, Q, T, R.

question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Many users pay only the minimum amount due, unaware of this.
Q. Credit cards offer an interest-free period of up to fifty days.
R. Their outstanding balance thus keeps growing month after month.
S. If the full bill is not paid by the due date, however, interest is charged at steep rates.
explanation: Q the feature, S the catch, P 'unaware of this', R the result.

question: The committee's findings were so _____ that the board had no choice but to _____ the chief executive.
explanation: Damning findings force a dismissal.

question: Far from _____ the crisis, the hasty announcement only served to _____ it.
explanation: 'Far from' sets up a contrast: it did not defuse but aggravated.

question: The new governor's _____ approach to inflation contrasted sharply with his predecessor's _____ stance.
explanation: A contrast needs opposite words: hawkish versus dovish.

question: Despite the _____ evidence against him, the accused continued to _____ his innocence.
explanation: 'Despite' needs strong evidence; one protests one's innocence.

question: The startup's _____ growth attracted investors, but its _____ accounting practices soon raised red flags.
explanation: Rapid growth attracts investors; dubious practices raise red flags.

question: The minister tried to _____ the protesters, but his _____ remarks only angered them further.
explanation: 'But' contrasts an attempt to calm with remarks that angered.

question: The scheme's benefits were _____ distributed, with a few large farmers _____ most of the subsidy.
explanation: A few cornering most of the benefit means uneven distribution.

question: The witness's account was _____ with the CCTV footage, which _____ doubts about his credibility.
explanation: A mismatch with the footage raises doubts.

question: _____ his reputation for frugality, the chairman approved a _____ budget for the annual celebrations.
explanation: A lavish budget contrasts with frugality, so a concessive word fits.

question: The regulator imposed a _____ penalty on the bank, signalling that it would no longer _____ lapses in KYC compliance.
explanation: A stiff penalty signals that lapses will no longer be tolerated.

question: The economist's forecast, once _____ as alarmist, has proved remarkably _____.
explanation: A forecast once dismissed has turned out to be prescient.

question: The talks _____ after both sides refused to _____ on the core issue of pricing.
explanation: Refusing to budge makes talks collapse.

question: The CEO's _____ remarks about the regulator were promptly _____ by the board, which issued a public apology.
explanation: An apology follows intemperate remarks the board disowns.

question: Only when the audit was complete _____ the full extent of the fraud _____.
explanation: 'Only when' triggers inversion with 'did' plus the base verb.

question: The new law is _____ to curb black money, but critics argue it will merely _____ honest taxpayers.
explanation: The stated aim contrasts with the critics' fear of harassment.

question: The professor was _____ in his praise, rarely _____ even his brightest students a compliment.
explanation: Rarely paying compliments means being sparing with praise.

question: The flood-hit villagers were left _____ after the waters _____ their homes and crops.
explanation: Losing homes and crops leaves people destitute.

question: The company's attempt to _____ its losses through creative accounting was _____ by an alert auditor.
explanation: Creative accounting conceals losses; an alert auditor exposes it.

question: As the deadline _____, the negotiators grew increasingly _____.
explanation: An approaching deadline makes people anxious.

question: The _____ of the new tax regime lies in its simplicity, which should _____ compliance among small traders.
explanation: Simplicity is a merit that improves compliance.

question: _____ the bank been adequately capitalised, it would not have _____ a government bailout.
explanation: Inverted third conditional: 'Had ... been', 'would not have required'.

question: The court _____ the petition as frivolous and _____ exemplary costs on the petitioner.
explanation: A frivolous petition is dismissed and costs are imposed.

question: The new CEO set about _____ the bloated bureaucracy, _____ several redundant layers of management.
explanation: Streamlining a bloated system means eliminating layers.

question: The documentary offers a _____ portrayal of rural poverty, neither _____ nor romanticising it.
explanation: A balanced portrayal avoids both sensationalising and romanticising.

question: Investors remained _____ about the merger, _____ the lack of clarity on the share-swap ratio.
explanation: Lack of clarity is cited as a reason for scepticism.

question: Though the drug showed _____ results in early trials, regulators _____ its approval pending larger studies.
explanation: 'Though' contrasts promising results with deferred approval.

question: The government's decision to _____ the ban on onion exports was _____ by farmers, who had lost heavily while it was in force.
explanation: Farmers hurt by the ban would welcome its lifting.

question: The athlete's _____ was called into question after he _____ a dope test.
explanation: Failing a dope test questions one's integrity.

question: With inflation _____, the central bank is expected to _____ rates to stimulate growth.
explanation: Easing inflation allows a rate cut to boost growth.

question: The inquiry report _____ the chairman of any wrongdoing, much to the _____ of his detractors.
explanation: Detractors are dismayed when the chairman is absolved.

question: The startup _____ its rivals by launching the product a full month _____ schedule.
explanation: Launching ahead of schedule lets it outpace rivals.

question: The bill was passed in _____, with barely any debate, prompting critics to call the process _____.
explanation: Passing a bill hastily without debate is called undemocratic.

question: The minister's _____ promises have bred _____ among voters, who no longer take him at his word.
explanation: Hollow promises breed cynicism.

question: So _____ was the speaker's argument that even his staunchest opponents found it hard to _____ it.
explanation: A cogent argument is hard to refute.

question: The project, plagued by cost _____ and delays, was eventually _____ by the new government.
explanation: A project plagued by overruns is likely to be scrapped.

question: Improve the part in capitals: The bank's new policy is DIFFERENT THAN the one introduced last year.
explanation: 'Different' is followed by 'from'.

question: Improve the part in capitals: The selection committee IS COMPRISED OF five members.
explanation: 'Comprise' means 'consist of' and takes no 'of'.

question: Improve the part in capitals: IT BEING a public holiday, the bank remained closed.
explanation: The absolute construction 'It being' is correct.

question: Improve the part in capitals: Not only HE PASSED the exam but also topped the state.
explanation: 'Not only' at the start requires inversion.

question: Improve the part in capitals: Each of the candidates WAS given a separate room.
explanation: 'Each of' takes a singular verb.

question: Improve the part in capitals: He AVAILED the opportunity to meet the chairman.
explanation: 'Avail' is used reflexively: 'avail oneself of'.

question: Improve the part in capitals: I am used TO WORK late hours during the audit season.
explanation: 'Be used to' is followed by a gerund.

question: Improve the part in capitals: Ten kilometres ARE a long distance to walk.
explanation: A plural amount taken as a single unit takes a singular verb.

question: Improve the part in capitals: Hardly ANY of the staff members turned up for the training.
explanation: 'Hardly' pairs with 'any', not with another negative.

question: Improve the part in capitals: He is ACCUSTOMED WITH the harsh climate of the hills.
explanation: 'Accustomed' takes the preposition 'to'.

question: Improve the part in capitals: She has been ABSENT FROM office since Monday.
explanation: 'Absent' takes 'from'.

question: Improve the part in capitals: I HAVE WRITTEN the letter to the manager yesterday.
explanation: A past time marker like 'yesterday' needs the simple past.

question: Improve the part in capitals: THE BOTH OF THEM were promoted last year.
explanation: 'Both' is not preceded by 'the'.

question: Improve the part in capitals: He gave me A VERY GOOD ADVICE on investments.
explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable and takes no article 'a'.

question: Improve the part in capitals: Kindly RETURN BACK the files by evening.
explanation: 'Return' already means 'come or give back'.

question: Improve the part in capitals: The meeting was postponed DUE TO the chairman was unwell.
explanation: A clause needs a conjunction like 'because', not a preposition.

question: Improve the part in capitals: Neither of the two applicants IS eligible for the post.
explanation: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb.

question: Improve the part in capitals: If he WERE to apply, he would surely be selected.
explanation: Hypothetical 'if ... were to' uses the subjunctive 'were'.

question: Improve the part in capitals: The more you practise, THE BETTER YOU WILL score in the exam.
explanation: 'The more ..., the better ...' is the correct paired comparative.

question: Improve the part in capitals: He said that he WILL VISIT the branch the next day.
explanation: Reported speech after a past reporting verb shifts 'will' to 'would'.

question: Improve the part in capitals: The jury WAS divided in their opinions.
explanation: A collective noun acting as individuals ('their opinions') takes a plural verb.

question: Improve the part in capitals: She has a GOOD COMMAND ON English.
explanation: 'Command' of a language takes 'of'.

question: Improve the part in capitals: All employees must abide BY the code of conduct.
explanation: 'Abide by' means to obey.

question: Improve the part in capitals: The cost of living HAS RISEN sharply this year.
explanation: The subject 'cost' is singular and 'risen' is the participle.

question: Improve the part in capitals: The officer enquired WHAT WAS MY NAME.
explanation: Indirect questions use statement word order.

question: Improve the part in capitals: Not a single customer WERE satisfied with the service.
explanation: 'Not a single' takes a singular verb.

question: Improve the part in capitals: The scheme WAS LAUNCHED by the minister in 2015.
explanation: A completed past action with a date takes the simple past.

question: Improve the part in capitals: The officer ORDERED FOR an inquiry into the matter.
explanation: 'Order' takes a direct object without 'for'.

question: Improve the part in capitals: One of the most important FACTOR AFFECTING loan demand is the interest rate.
explanation: 'One of the most' takes a plural noun.

question: Improve the part in capitals: My new colleague DOES NOT KNOW TO DRIVE a car.
options: does not know how to drive
explanation: 'Know' needs 'how to' before an infinitive of skill.

question: Choose the word closest in meaning to the word in capitals: The OBDURATE official refused every request for reconsideration.
explanation: Obdurate means stubbornly refusing to change.

question: Choose the word closest in meaning to the word in capitals: The board was criticised for its PUSILLANIMOUS response to the fraud.
explanation: Pusillanimous means lacking courage.

question: Choose the word closest in meaning to the word in capitals: The bank detected several SPURIOUS notes in the cash chest.
explanation: Spurious means false or fake.

question: Choose the word closest in meaning to the word in capitals: Her ASSIDUOUS preparation earned her the top rank.
explanation: Assiduous means showing great care and persistence.

question: Choose the word closest in meaning to the word in capitals: What seemed an INNOCUOUS remark sparked a heated debate.
explanation: Innocuous means not harmful or offensive.

question: Choose the word closest in meaning to the word in capitals: The lecture on derivatives was too ABSTRUSE for the trainees.
explanation: Abstruse means difficult to understand.

question: Choose the word closest in meaning to the word in capitals: Crop insurance helps MITIGATE the losses caused by drought.
explanation: Mitigate means make less severe.

question: Choose the word closest in meaning to the word in capitals: The governor adopted a PRAGMATIC approach to the crisis.
explanation: Pragmatic means dealing with things sensibly and realistically.

question: Choose the word closest in meaning to the word in capitals: Her business ACUMEN helped the firm survive the recession.
explanation: Acumen means keen insight and judgement.

question: Choose the word closest in meaning to the word in capitals: Delays in disbursal only EXACERBATED the farmers' distress.
explanation: Exacerbate means make worse.

question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The reforms were meant to AMELIORATE living conditions in the slums.

question: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct? (Set 21)
options: Scarcely had the train left when it began to rain.
Scarcely had the train left than it began to rain.
Scarcely the train had left when it began to rain.
Scarcely did the train left when it began to rain.
explanation: 'Scarcely had ... when' is the correct pattern.

question: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct? (Set 22)

He is one of the best officers that have ever served here.
He is one of the best officer that have ever served here.
He is one of best officers that has ever served here.
explanation: The relative pronoun refers to the plural 'officers', so the verb is plural.

question: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct? (Set 23)

question: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct? (Set 24)

He as well as his friends were guilty.
He as well as his friends have been guilty.
He as well as his friends is guilty.
